items.title: How do we know when invasive species control strategies work?
items.abstract: Controlling invasive species is costly and difficult but can have major ecological, economic, and health benefits. Researchers commonly compare the efficacy of specific control methods. However, invasive species control programs vary greatly in overarching goals and often occur over large areas, long timeframes, and varied environmental and social contexts. The success of these programs likely hinges on factors including organizational structures, concurrent restoration activities, geographic and temporal scope of control, and the invasive species’ biology. To enable assessment of the relative influence of these common features, we propose clearer definitions of success in invasive species control and explicit comparisons among control programs. Post hoc assessment of existing programs’ success will complement system-specific studies to guide strategies that work in real-world situations.

items.title: The interplay of landscape connectivity, composition and configuration in alien plant invasions across an ecological network
items.abstract: Context Biological invasions are deemed to be the second most important global driver of biodiversity loss showing strong interactions with the aftermaths of land use change and landscape fragmentation. The role of landscape composition and configuration in biological invasions is widely considered while its interplay with landscape connectivity is less understood. However, ecological connectivity can be equally crucial for both native and alien species, constituting the backbone of ecological network initiatives. Objectives We aim to assess how landscape composition, configuration and connectivity (in the ecological network) influence α- and β-diversity (floristic uniqueness) of both alien and native plant species, and to determine whether these effects differ according to habitat type. Methods The study was conducted in a 298 km 2 ecological network in the lowlands of Friuli Venezia Giulia, northeastern Italy, encompassing a mosaic of agricultural, natural, and semi-natural habitats. A hierarchical sampling design was applied to 87 terrestrial habitat nodes, where plant species composition and abundance were recorded in 219 plots. Landscape composition, configuration and connectivity were quantified to examine their influence on native and alien plant α- and β-diversity across different habitat types. Results We found contrasting effects of landscape connectivity, composition and configuration for native and alien species. Peripheral, less connected sites favored native species richness (α-diversity) and contributed to maintaining native floristic uniqueness (high β-diversity). In contrast, alien species richness was mainly associated with landscape composition and configuration, particularly the proportion of natural land use and edge-related effects in wooded habitats, while plots with higher alien richness showed lower compositional uniqueness within the alien species pool. Landscape composition and configuration also influenced invasion dynamics, as nodes surrounded by a high proportion of natural land uses with simple shapes helped contain plant invasions while preserving native richness and uniqueness. These patterns were often habitat-dependent, with stronger effects observed in wooded areas, where alien α-diversity increased with fragmentation, whereas native species richness declined. Conclusions Our findings suggest that managing landscape connectivity and reducing fragmentation can enhance resistance to invasions and support native species richness. Peripheral nodes may act as native refugia, supporting high native richness and floristic uniqueness, while more accessible central nodes may function as alien hubs associated with greater alien compositional uniqueness and potential propagule exchange. Shifting from intensive to extensive land uses through green infrastructures provides a win–win strategy, promoting native species and limit alien establishment.

items.title: The science-policy gap on invasive species management: a review of research capacity, regulations, and data availability for an intergovernmental framework in the gulf cooperation council
items.abstract: Invasive alien species (IAS) pose major threats to biodiversity, ecosystem function, and agriculture, undermining progress on the Sustainable Development Goals. The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), with its arid climate, rapid urbanisation, dependence on imports, and ecologically fragile, endemic-rich habitats, is especially vulnerable. This paper constructs bridges over the science–policy gap in invasive species management through a systematic review of national and regional regulatory frameworks, global invasion ecology publications, and 3.9 million biodiversity records. GCC institutions contribute only 0.6% of global invasion-ecology publications and, when normalised by GDP, produce invasion science at less than one-third of the global rate. Across the GCC, only 84 of 707 GRIIS-listed IAS (11.9%) are regulated, despite significant economic impacts. Critical deficiencies include species-specific laws, pathway controls, enforcement, and cross-border coordination, as most nations address invasive species only within broader biodiversity strategies. To remedy this, we propose an Inter-Governmental Invasive Species Science-Policy Platform (IISSPP), modelled on the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES), a lean intergovernmental science–policy platform built around regular assessments, early warning and knowledge generation, policy support, and capacity building. IISSPP would harmonise regulations, standardise risk assessments, unify watch lists, and promote open data sharing. The IISSPP model is replicable in other rapidly developing regions and supports global biodiversity targets under the Kunming–Montreal Framework while advancing regional sustainable development and climate resilience.

items.title: Integrating land-use and climate connectivity to link protected areas at the country level
items.abstract: Context Ecological corridors that are high in biodiversity potential and stable under climate change are central to long-term conservation planning. Yet spatial prioritization frameworks rarely integrate land-use resistance and climate stability into a unified approach, limiting their operational value for landscape management and policy. Objectives We aimed to develop an ecological connectivity framework that jointly incorporates land-use resistance and climate stability to map linkages among protected areas, and to quantify and communicate methodological uncertainty arising from key parameterization choices. Methods We applied the framework to Portugal's terrestrial protected-area network. Using a full factorial design, we varied land-use resistance, climate resistance, and dispersal capacity across multiple weightings to generate optimized linkage solutions. Selection-frequency maps derived from these solutions fed a second optimization round, producing an ensemble connectivity solution and buffered corridors. Results Individual solutions covered 0.74% of Portugal's unprotected land; the ensemble covered 0.07%, rising to 2.3% after a 1 km buffer. Dispersal capacity parameterization introduced greater uncertainty in connectivity outcomes than land-use or climate resistance scores, suggesting it deserves particular attention in future studies. Protected areas in the Central–North region emerged as the most critical network hubs, with the highest centrality under both resistance gradients. The ensemble highlighted areas of high concordance across parameterizations, improving the robustness of spatial priorities. Conclusions Integrating land-use and climate resistance identifies corridors that are both functional and climate-resilient. Explicitly mapping uncertainty and producing ensemble-prioritized linkages improves the reliability of spatial recommendations, offering planners a practical tool for embedding connectivity targets into conservation and land management decisions.

items.title: A standardized workflow for compiling and harmonizing first records of non-native species
items.abstract: NeoBiota 110: 1-20 DOI: 10.3897/neobiota.110.198728 Authors: Tanara Renard Truong, Franz Essl, Hanno Seebens Abstract: Biological invasions are a major driver of biodiversity loss, and tracking non-native species introductions is essential for biodiversity monitoring and policy assessment. First records, defined as the earliest documented evidence of a species occurring in the wild outside its native range, provide a standardized metric to quantify introduction dynamics across regions and taxonomic groups. However, compiling and harmonizing such records from diverse sources remain challenging due to non-standardized terminology and heterogeneous reporting standards. Here, we describe a reproducible workflow for standardizing first records of non-native species from diverse sources. The workflow is implemented in R and is designed to ensure consistency in taxonomy, harmonize geographic locations, convert heterogeneous temporal expressions into four-digit years using explicit transformation rules, and standardize terms following Darwin Core terminology. A key innovation of the workflow is the assignment of a confidence level to each standardized first record, reflecting the uncertainty of the original temporal information. The workflow is open-source, modular, and customizable, allowing users to apply it to their own data or modify standardization rules. It is applied to produce v4.0 of the FirstRecords dataset, which contains nearly 100,000 first records of more than 30,000 taxa and is structured into linked tables covering actual records, taxonomy, locations, and data sources. This represents a 17.8% increase in the amount of available first records compared to the previous version, of which approximately 8% is due to the refinement of the workflow. By providing a transparent and automated approach to data harmonization, this workflow facilitates large-scale analyses of invasion patterns and indicator development, while maintaining data integrity. items.title: Spatial and historical effects shape a wide‐scale rice field ostracod metacommunity pervaded by invasive species
items.abstract: Metacommunity structure is shaped by a complex interplay of environmental conditions, spatial factors, and historical contingencies. To determine the processes that govern community assembly and biodiversity patterns, it is necessary to know the relative importance of these elements. In this study, we examine the ostracod metacommunity of rice fields across the Iberian Peninsula, aiming to assess the influence of spatial constraints, historical contingency (as derived from taphocoenoses remains), and environmental variables on the present metacommunity (biocoenoses) structure. We hypothesized that while all three components would affect the metacommunity, spatial effects would be particularly relevant due to the large geographical scope and associated dispersal limitations. Our results indicate that space was the most relevant factor in structuring the metacommunity, operating at broad and fine scales. Historical contingency also contributed substantially, as indicated by the high concordance between taphocoenoses and biocoenoses, suggesting that past community composition influences present assemblages, possibly through colonization advantages associated with egg banks. Although the pure environmental fraction was comparatively weak and nonsignificant, likely due to the low environmental variability of these homogeneous and artificially controlled aquatic habitats, the substantial shared environmental-spatial fraction could indicate that environmental conditions covaried with broad-scale spatial structure among regions. A notable number of invasive ostracods were identified, suggesting ongoing, albeit infrequent, colonization processes, probably facilitated by waterbirds, land ploughing, movement of agricultural machinery, and farmer activities, which support the establishment of invasive species within each community egg bank. These findings indicate that biodiversity management in seasonal agricultural landscapes, such as rice fields, should extend beyond local environmental conditions, taking into account regional connectivity, the persistence of egg-bank legacies, and human-mediated dispersal pathways that may facilitate the establishment of non-native species.

items.title: Resource subsidies mediated by non-native species: a review
items.abstract: NeoBiota 109: 315-343 DOI: 10.3897/neobiota.109.193175 Authors: Letícia Alves, Janeide Padilha, Phillip J. Haubrock, Amanda Subalusky, Ronaldo Sousa Abstract: Non-native species are recognized as one of the major drivers of biodiversity change globally, with profound impacts on ecosystem functions and services. Despite the high number of studies on non-native species published, mainly in the last two decades, an often-overlooked aspect is their role as mediators of resource subsidies (the cross-boundary movement of energy, nutrients, or materials). This topic may have theoretical and empirical implications because non-native species may play a major role in ecosystem connectivity by transporting—or interrupting the transport of—energy and organic matter. Therefore, the main aims of this review were to (1) assess temporal trends, geographic distribution, and methodological approaches in research on resource subsidies mediated by non-native species; (2) synthesize how non-native species alter the magnitude, direction, and dynamics of resource subsidies across ecosystems and their implications for ecosystem functioning; and (3) identify key gaps in current knowledge and define future research priorities. The review retrieved 143 publications, resulting in 212 case studies, that collectively show that non-native species can both reduce and increase resource flows across ecosystem boundaries, with implications for ecosystem dynamics and connectivity. Although terrestrial and freshwater connectivity accounted for the majority of published case studies (56%), many ecosystem linkages remain underexplored. A significant geographic bias was found, with Africa being severely understudied (2.8% of all publications), followed by Asia (7.7% of all publications). Taxonomic representation was also skewed, with the majority of studies focusing on non-native plants (28.8% of case studies), non-native fish (25.5% of case studies), and mammals (21.7% of case studies), whereas fungi (0.9%) and bacteria (2.4%) were largely neglected despite their fundamental roles in decomposition processes. Key priorities for advancing this field include long-term monitoring, the application of emerging molecular and analytical tools (e.g., telemetry, eDNA, metabarcoding, and isotopic tracers), and the integration of artificial intelligence to synthesize large datasets. The findings provide the first synthesis of resource subsidies mediated by non-native species. This information is crucial for biodiversity conservation and the effective management of ecosystems and their connectivity. HTML XML PDF

items.title: Effects of climate change on marine biodiversity on the western Atlantic coast
items.abstract: The current climate crisis, driven by greenhouse gas emissions, threatens global biodiversity, including that in marine ecosystems. However, projections for the western Atlantic Ocean that jointly quantify species richness and endemism while accounting for spatially biased and incomplete occurrence data remain limited. We addressed this gap across the western Atlantic from 57°S to 40°N, within 1500 km of the coast and on the continental shelf in waters shallower than 150 m. Using broad taxonomic coverage across vertebrates, invertebrates, and algae, we modeled biodiversity metrics directly as species richness and the corrected weighted endemism index (WEIc), applied uniform sampling from sampling effort (USSE) to minimize the effects of spatially biased and incomplete occurrence records on predictions, and tested multiple algorithms to project these metrics under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 for 2050 and 2100. The results indicated a significant reduction in species richness and endemism, with up to 69% of the study area projected to experience a reduction of more than 5% in species richness under the high-emissions scenarios. The most affected areas included the coast of Florida, the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean, the northern region of South America, and southern Brazil. The decrease in endemism was equally concerning, with significant reductions predicted in areas of high diversity, threatening species adapted to specific ecological niches and increasing the risk of local extinctions. Vertebrates and invertebrates showed the greatest reductions in richness in the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean, northeastern Brazil, and northern Argentina. For algae, the most significant decreases were predicted for Florida and southern Brazil. This loss of biodiversity could compromise the resilience of marine ecosystems and the availability of fishery resources, highlighting the urgent need for coordinated global actions.

items.title: Legacy effects of land use land cover change on species distribution dynamics: evidence from a landscape of diverse biogeographic crossroads
items.abstract: Context Land use and land cover (LULC) change is a key driver of biodiversity distribution, yet species responses vary among taxa, habitats, and regions. Because species responses are context-dependent, understanding how ecological characteristics and landscape history influence biodiversity distribution is essential for conservation planning. Objectives We evaluated how nearly two centuries of LULC change have influenced vertebrate distribution dynamics across Texas, USA, a landscape of biogeographic crossroads. We tested whether habitat specialization, taxonomic identity, conservation status, and ecoregional context better explain range expansion, contraction, and redistribution than landscape change metrics alone. Methods We compared historical and contemporary distributions of 100 native vertebrate species (mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians). Multi-temporal LULC datasets (1850–2023) were integrated with species occurrences, habitat associations, and ecoregional data to identify drivers of distribution range change. Results LULC change was spatially heterogeneous, driven by agricultural expansion, cropland abandonment, shrubland encroachment, and urbanization. Most species shifted ranges, with responses varying by habitat, taxon, and ecoregion. Habitat specialists, reptiles, and amphibians showed the greatest contractions, whereas birds were comparably stable or expanding, with responses differing among ecoregions. Habitat affinity, vertebrate class, and ecoregional identity were stronger predictors of range change than landscape transformation metrics alone. Conclusions LULC legacies set the environmental template and influence species distributions indirectly through ecological filtering, species-specific traits, and regional context rather than change magnitude alone. By linking historical landscape trajectories with contemporary biodiversity patterns, this study provides a useful template for understanding land use legacies, species redistribution, and community reassembly in diverse landscapes, emphasizing adaptive capacity and connectivity for conservation planning.
